review: We went in the first week of August and the valley was carpeted with blue poppies, cobra lilies and balsam. Gaurav knew the name of almost every flower and never rushed the slower walkers. The climb to Hemkund Sahib was hard, but the lake at the top made up for it.

Beautiful trek and very well run. It rained on two afternoons, which is normal in the monsoon, and the team had ponchos and hot tea ready at Ghangaria. The guesthouse there is basic, so pack a warm layer for the night.

My first Himalayan trek and I felt looked after from Rishikesh to the last day. Rohit carried my bag up the final stretch to Hemkund when the altitude got to me. I came back with more flower photos than I know what to do with.

The valley itself is a five, no question. The drive from Rishikesh to Joshimath on the first day is long, and a landslide held us up for two hours, but the team stayed calm and adjusted the plan without any fuss.

Summit day started at 3 a.m. in knee-deep snow and ended with sunrise over Swargarohini and Bandarpoonch. Gaurav set a steady pace and made us stop to rest before we needed it, which is why everyone in the group reached the top.
Camping at Juda Ka Talab with the frozen lake next to our tents was magical. The tents and sleeping bags kept us warm at minus eight, and the kitchen team somehow made hot jalebis in the snow.

A great winter trek for beginners who are reasonably fit. The drive from Dehradun to Sankri is long and bumpy, so plan to rest that evening. Microspikes were provided and we really needed them on the way down.
The trek was lovely, but our batch was larger than I expected and the toilet tents at base camp were stretched. The guides were excellent. I would go again with a smaller group.

Two full days in Leh before going higher made all the difference, and nobody in our group got sick. Crossing Khardung La, the double-humped camels at Hunder and the colours of Pangong at sunset were the highlights. Tsering's stories about growing up in Leh made the long drives fly by.
Spectacular landscapes and a careful, safety-first team. Expect long days in the vehicle and a cold night at Pangong, where the camp had electricity for only a few hours. Worth every rupee.
Rigzin arranged an early visit to Thiksey for the morning prayers, which was the most peaceful hour of the whole trip. There was oxygen in every vehicle and our driver was superb on the passes.
I was nervous about the altitude at 58, but the pace and the rest days were very well planned. My only wish is one more night in Nubra.

The night at Langza was the clearest sky I have ever seen. Deepika set up a telescope beside the Buddha statue and showed us Saturn's rings. Key Monastery and the drive past Chandra Taal were bonuses.
Rough roads and simple homestays, as you would expect in Spiti, but our hosts in Kibber were wonderful and the food was hot and filling. Bring a power bank, because charging is patchy.
Posting a postcard from Hikkim and finding fossils at Langza felt like a school trip for grown-ups. The guides checked everyone's oxygen levels at Kunzum and Kaza and never hurried us.
Unreal landscapes, and the stargazing was the best part, although we lost one night to cloud. The team made up for it with an extra session the following evening.

Fort Kochi in the morning, tea estates in Munnar by evening and a night on a houseboat near Alappuzha: three very different sides of Kerala in five days. Anjali's food tips were spot on, especially the karimeen pollichathu.
We saw Nilgiri tahr up close at Eravikulam and walked through a tea estate with a planter who explained every step of the process. The houseboat crew cooked the best appam I have ever had.
Relaxed and well paced, perfect for travelling with our parents. The drive between Munnar and Alappuzha is long and winding, so carry travel sickness tablets if you need them.
Kumarakom at sunrise, with birds all over Vembanad Lake, was pure calm. Sneha handled every booking, ticket and boat transfer, so we never waited around.
Sleeping under the stars at Sam after a camel ride at sunset was the high point of my year. Karan's history of Jaisalmer Fort, where families still live inside the walls, was fascinating.
Desert nights in January are properly cold, so the extra blankets at the camp were welcome. The folk music around the fire was a lovely touch. The camel ride is bumpy, so wear long trousers.
Kuldhara at dusk was eerie in the best way. The food was rich Rajasthani thalis every day. I loved the ker sangri but was craving something lighter by day three.
Well organised from the station pickup to the drop. Arvind spotted a desert fox near the dunes and a chinkara on the drive back, which none of us expected.
Radhanagar Beach at sunset lives up to the hype. The snorkelling trip off Havelock showed us more fish and coral than I imagined. The ferries ran on time and the team handled all the tickets.
The light and sound show at the Cellular Jail was moving and gave the whole trip more meaning. Neil Island was quieter than Havelock and ended up being our favourite.
Gorgeous water and an easy pace. The Port Blair hotel was ordinary next to the beach resorts, and ferry transfers take up a lot of time, but that is the nature of island hopping.

I am not a strong swimmer, and Sneha stayed next to me for the whole snorkel, which gave me the confidence to enjoy it. Ross Island's ruins, with deer and peacocks wandering through them, were a lovely surprise.

Seeing the Taj Mahal at sunrise before the crowds arrived was unforgettable, and Imran knew exactly where to stand for photos. Humayun's Tomb in Delhi was the surprise of the trip: calm, huge and often overlooked.
A lot of history in six days. The expressway makes Delhi to Agra easy, but Agra to Jaipur via Fatehpur Sikri is a long day. Amber Fort and the stepwell nearby were superb.
Karan took us to a small family-run place in Old Delhi after Jama Masjid, and that food walk was a highlight. The hotels were comfortable and central.
Great guides and well-timed visits. The shopping stop in Jaipur felt long, but when we asked to skip it and walk to Hawa Mahal instead, the team happily arranged it.
Kangchenjunga turned pink at sunrise from Tiger Hill and the whole crowd went silent. The tea tasting afterwards finally taught me the difference between a first and a second flush.
The toy train to Ghum and around the Batasia Loop was charming. Roads into Sikkim are slow, so the long driving days are tiring, but Pelling's mountain views made up for it.

Temi Tea Garden was my favourite stop: rolling green slopes, low cloud drifting through the bushes and hardly any other visitors. Suraj knew the story behind every monastery we visited, especially Rumtek.
A lovely mix of tea, mountains and monasteries. Tsomgo Lake was still partly frozen in late April, and the cold at over 3,700 metres surprised a few of us, so bring a proper jacket.
We saw a tigress with two cubs on our second safari, near one of the lakes. Arvind read every alarm call from the langurs and sambar and had the jeep in exactly the right place.

Two of our four safaris had no tiger sightings, which is how wildlife works, but we saw crocodiles, owls, a sloth bear in the distance and dozens of birds. The fort walk was a great break between drives.
A tiger walking slowly along the track at dusk, ten metres from our jeep, is a sight I will never forget. The naturalist kept everyone quiet and patient, and it paid off.
Short, efficient and well planned. The lodge was comfortable, and the team packed breakfast boxes for the early morning safaris.

The steps down to the double-decker root bridge at Nongriat are hard on the knees, but swimming in the blue pools below was worth it. Wanphrang explained how Khasi families grow these bridges over generations.
The Umngot at Dawki is so clear that the boats look as if they are floating in the air. Mawlynnong was spotless and the villagers were welcoming.
Plan for rain even outside the monsoon; Sohra lived up to its reputation. Nohkalikai Falls was huge even in March. The homestay at Nongriat was simple, but the family cooking was excellent.
Shillong's cafes, Khasi food and the friendliest guides. Pema made sure everyone had a walking stick for the stairs. I did not expect to love the northeast this much.

Sunrise from Matanga Hill over the boulders and temples was the best hour of the trip. Kavya's knowledge of the Vijayanagara kings brought the ruins to life, and the stone chariot at the Vittala Temple is even finer in person.
Hampi is huge, so cycling on day two was a smart idea. It gets hot by noon even in January, and the plan of exploring early and resting after lunch worked well.
The coracle ride on the Tungabhadra and the climb up Anjanadri Hill were great fun. Our guesthouse looked out over the paddy fields, which was the perfect place to end each day.
Well organised, though the drive in from Hosapete on the first morning took longer than expected. Anjali adjusted the order of the sites so we still saw everything on the list.
Rafting from Shivpuri through rapids like Roller Coaster and Golf Course was a rush, and the safety briefing was thorough. The evening aarti at Triveni Ghat was a peaceful way to end the day.
A good mix of adventure and calm. The rafting was the main event, and the Beatles Ashram walk the next morning was more interesting than I expected. Lunch by the river was simple but filling.
Rohit was a calm, funny raft captain and kept the nervous swimmers relaxed. April is a great month to go: the water was cold but not freezing.
A great short break from Delhi. Ram Jhula on a weekend was very crowded, so the early morning walk the guides suggested was the right call.
